title: Appendix A — Draft: Data Documentation
text:
Goal is to give evidence to my boss that shark-infested storms are very rare, if not impossible.
The data I found is from the NOAA data base. I extracted tornado data from Los Angeles (the setting of Sharknado), Florida (tropical storms are abundant), South Carolina (another more tropical place), and Oklahoma (the tornado capitol of the nation).
All the data sets are the same format. They were collected from the same data base NOAA.gov.
These are the important aspects of the data sets collected

County Location
Begin Location
Begin Date
Begin Time
Tornado F Scale
Direct Deaths
Direct Injuries
Property Damage
Tornado Length and Width
End Location
End Date
End Time

Measurements are take by the MWS Storm Survey, Spotters, State officials and the Public

Florida tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.a)
South Carolina tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.b)
Oklahoma tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.c)
Los Angeles tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.d)

For a tornado to lift up a Shark I compared the weight of a Great White Shark to a normal cars weight

Great White Shark Weight

NOAA Says up to 4,500 lbs

Car weight

According to autoinsurance.com a Car SUV is 3,986 lbs
According to autoinsurance.com a Truck SUV is 4,578 lbs

Great White Sharks and Car SUVs and Truck SUVs weigh relatively around the same weight.

oteroadjusting.com says EF3 tornadoes are likely to toss cars and trucks and EF5 can “almost certainly lift and destroy cars.”
I will use this as a reference to say that EF3-EF5 tornadoes will be able to lift a great white shark.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
To see if a Sharknado can actually happen first we need to see how a great white shark could be able to be picked up by a tornado. We will be looking at the weight of a great white shark first and compare it to other objects that can and have been picked up by tornadoes, cars. Next we need to figure out what strength (in EF scale from EF3 - EF5) of a tornado would be needed to be able to lift a great white shark and a car. Lastly, we are going to look at some tornados from 2015-2026 that are in the desired EF scale range (EF3-EF5) from 4 different places in the United States. These places are going to be Florida, South Carolina, Oklahoma, and Los Angeles. These places were chosen for specific reasons. Florida has many tropical storms and a coastal state. South Carolina is also another place that can be hit by tropical storms and is another coastal state. Oklahoma is not a coastal state but it is the tornado capital of the United States so we will just be looking at the amount of tornadoes that fit our criteria. Los Angeles was picked because that is the setting of the Sharknado movie.
Sharks and cars weigh relatively the same in pounds (lbs). The average great white shark weighs around 4,500 lbs according to NOAA. A car SUV weighs around 3,986 lbs while a truck SUV costs around 4,578 lbs according to autoinsurance.com. This means that your average great white shark weighs more than a big car and as much as a truck SUV. We will use a car as the base to find what EF scale level will be used to lift a great white shark out of water.
The EF scale is made up of 6 different ratings of tornado based on 3 second wind speed in mph. An EF0 tornado is has the lowest wind speed ranging between 65-85 mph, EF1 has winds speeds between 86-110 mph, EF2 has wind speeds between 111-135 mph, EF3 has wind speeds of 136-165 mph, EF4 has speeds between 166-200 mph and EF5 has wind speed that are over 200 mph. According to oteroadjusting.com, an EF3 tornado is likely to toss cars and trucks, while an EF4 is very likely to toss cars many feet, and an EF5 tornado is almost certain to lift and destroy cars. Since we are comparing a great white shark to the size and weight of a car SUV and a truck SUV that gives us a good comparison to be able to put a shark in the place of those cars in the EF scales ability to lift cars. We are going to look at tornadoes that are only EF3 to EF5 because those are the strength of tornadoes that are able to lift a car.
Lets take a look at some tornado data from a tropical place that gets some pretty bad storms regularly in Florida. Florida is also a place that is on the coast so it would be able to pick up a shark in the event of a strong enough tornado.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
tornado_fl <- read.csv("tornado_data_florida.csv")

tornado_fl$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", tornado_fl$TOR_F_SCALE)
tornado_fl <- tornado_fl|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)|>
  filter(
    TOR_F_SCALE > 2
  )

tornado_fl |>
  gt()

Figure B.1: Florida Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data




Figure B.1 shows that there have been only 5 EF3 tornadoes in the last 10 years in the state of Florida. Because of an EF3 tornado being the highest EF rating and it being “likely to toss a car or truck” we can believe that a tornado in Florida is pretty unlikely to pick up the average great white shark. Having only five EF3 tornadoes in the past 10 years seems like the chances of a Sharknado happening look pretty slim.

Figure B.2: South Carolina Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data




Looking at Figure B.2 South Carolina is similar to Florida. There are a lot of EF3 tornadoes with one EF4 tornado. But it’s in the same boat as Florida, there has been a very limited number of powerful tornadoes over the past 10 years for South Carolina. There has been nine EF3 tornadoes and one EF4 tornado over that span. The surprising thing is that the one EF4 and six of the EF3 tornadoes all happened on the same day. But the possibility of a sharknado is very low because these tornadoes all happened away from the coast. The EF4 happened in the Estill and Hampton Counties.
Next let’s look at a place that has a ton of tornadoes so we can get a good comparison of the strength of tornadoes in a very tornado heavy area in Oklahoma.

From Figure B.3 we are only looking at the ten highest EF scale tornadoes to hit Oklahoma because there are 27 tornadoes in the EF3 to EF5 rating. The ten highest tornadoes in Oklahoma over the last 10 years have been two EF5 tornadoes, seven EF4 tornadoes, and one EF3 tornado. This tells us that EF5s are a very rare occurrence even for the tornado capital of the country.
To make a real connection to the Sharknado movie we should look at the actual setting of the movie which is Los Angeles, California. Looking at tornadoes in LA to give us a real idea of the possible strength of some tornadoes that have hit Los Angeles over the past ten years.

Figure B.4: California Tornado Data




Looking at Figure B.4 above we can see all of the tornado data over the last ten years in Los Angeles. As you can see there have been only EF0 and EF1 tornadoes to hit Los Angeles over this span of time. By comparing the levels of EF ratings specified before (needing between EF3 - EF5), we can see there is not really a possibility of getting a tornado with wind speeds strong enough to pick up a shark to create a Sharknado. From https://science.howstuffworks.com/, they say the mph of wind speed needed to lift a shark off the ground is about 200 mph. The wind speed of an EF0 tornado is between 65 - 85 mph while an EF1 tornado has wind speeds between 86 - 110 mph. This shows us that we are barely able to get to half the wind speed of the speed needed to pick a shark up off the ground in Los Angeles.
Lets compare all of the tornadoes for each location we chose (Florida, South Carolina, Oklahoma, Los Angeles) with an EF scale rating of EF3 to EF5 and compare to see which places have the best chance to start a Sharknado by looking at a stacked bar chart. Note that Los Angeles only has EF0 and EF1 tornadoes so we will use those only in this chart.

all_tornado <- bind_rows(
  tornado_fl,
  tornado_sc,
  tornado_ok_10,
  tornado_la
)

ggplot(all_tornado, aes(x = STATE_ABBR, fill = factor(TOR_F_SCALE))) +
  geom_bar()+
    scale_fill_discrete(
    name = "Tornado Strength",
    labels = c("EF0","EF1","EF3","EF4","EF5")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10,by = 2)) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure B.5: Bar Chart for Tornadoes Higher than EF3 Over Last 10 Years for FL, SC, and OK, All Tornadoes Over Last 10 Years for CA





This graph allows us to look at the strength of each locations tornadoes on the EF scale compared to each other. According to science.howstuffworks.com/, the wind speed needed to lift a shark off the ground is 200 mph. An EF3 tornado has wind speeds of 136-165 mph, an EF4 tornado has speeds between 166-200 mph and an EF5 tornado has wind speeds that are over 200 mph. This means that an EF5 tornado is only strong enough to lift a shark off the ground. As we can see there have only been two tornadoes in the last ten years that have been strong enough to have wind speeds of 200 mph or more. So there were only two tornadoes that have been strong enough to be able to pick up a shark but they happened in Oklahoma. That means there is no chance that there is a possibility that a Sharknado can happen in Florida, South Carolina, or Los Angeles. But in Oklahoma there might be a possibility of a Sharknado. At the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks, OK there is Shark Adventure which is home to ten of the “most dangerous sharks known to man”. These sharks are bull sharks. Jenks, OK is in Tulsa County, so let’s look at some tornadoes over the last 10 years for Tulsa County, Oklahoma.

Looking at the tornadoes that have gone through Tulsa County Oklahoma we can see that the tornadoes don’t reach EF3 or higher at all. But Bull Sharks only weigh around 500 lbs. This means that they are much easier for a tornado to lift up than a great white shark. According to https://www.oreateai.com/, an EF2 tornado has the strength to slightly move houses off its foundations and destroy mobile homes. If an EF2 tornado went through the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks and destroyed the aquarium it could potentially pick up sharks from the “most dangerous sharks known to man” exhibit to create a real life Sharknado. Thinking of this logic this could also apply to a lot of other aquariums throughout the country. But the chances of this happening is relatively low. The last time a tornado hit an aquarium was in 2024 when an EF1 tornado went through the Pittsburgh Zoo & Aquarium. This only resulted in some damage to the property and some trees to get knocked over. Thinking about the possibility of a Sharknado is pretty slim when there is record of a tornado that went through an aquarium there was still not a chance.

D Introduction
This study goes over the idea the possibility of a Sharknado scenario for insurance payouts for property damage purposes. A Sharknado is explained by a tornado that generates enough wind speed to be able to lift a heavy animal, such as a great white shark, out of the water and into its vortex. A Sharknado can also be called a “Shark infested tornado”.
This study starts by comparing the average great white shark to objects of similar weight specifically cars or pickup trucks. Tornadoes are known for destroying homes and tossing around vehicles thus finding the types of vehicles that are similar enough in weight to a great white shark makes finding the right magnitude of tornadoes required to lift a great white shark easier.
Next, finding the magnitude of a tornado capable of picking up a great white shark, or a car, is found using the EF scale (Enhanced Fujita Scale) by looking at EF ratings (US Department of Commerce (n.d.)). The Enhanced Fujita Scale uses rating of EF0 to EF5. Tornadoes of interest for this study are tornadoes of rating EF3 to EF5. These tornadoes have strong enough wind speeds to potentially pick up and throw cars or, in this case, a great white shark.
Finally, looking at places that are near the coast to be able to pick up a great white shark is essential to actually generating a Sharknado. There are 3 locations observed for their tornado data that fit this agenda in this study. Those places being Florida, South Carolina, and Los Angeles (this is the setting of the Sharknado movie). For another comparison of tornado strength Oklahoma is also looked at for tornado EF rating. These locations are have tornado data taken from 2015 - 2026 using NOAA tornado data.
By combining the magnitude of tornadoes with the areas where these tornadoes touched down gives an idea to the possibility of a potential Sharknado event occurring.

title: Appendix D — Draft: Executive Summary
text:
E Executive Summary

E.0.1 Purpose of Report
This study dives into the possibility of a Sharknado event. A Sharknado can be explained as a “shark infested tornado”. This is a tornado that generates enough wind speed to lift a great white shark from the water and into its vortex. The purpose of this study is to assess a Sharknado event could be considered as a risk for property damage insurance pay outs.


E.0.2 Methods
To start, a comparison of the weight of a great white shark (around 4500 lbs) and vehicles (around 4000 - 4600 lbs for SUV and Trucks) is used because cars are known to be lifted and destroyed by tornadoes. Using the EF (Enhanced Fujita) Scale the strength of tornado able to lift and toss cars (or a great white shark) is found to be between EF3 - EF5 tornadoes. This is wind speeds of 136 mph to 200+ mph. This study will only be looking at tornadoes of EF3 - EF5 because of this reason. This study also looks at four locations of tornado data from 2015-2026. These locations are Florida, South Carolina, Oklahoma, California, and Los Angeles County, CA. These places were chosen because of their abundant tropical storms and coastal area (Florida and South Carolina), historic tornado amounts and strength (Oklahoma), and the setting of the movie Sharknado (Los Angeles, CA).


E.0.3 Findings
Tornadoes of strength EF3 - EF5 are fairly uncommon for coastal states like Florida, and South Carolina. Florida had only five tornadoes in the last 10 years that are of strength EF3 and zero EF4 and EF5 tornadoes. All but one of these tornadoes are started started and ended on land. The one tornado other tornado started on a beach in Florida where the water is not deep enough for sharks. South Carolina had nine EF3 and one EF4 tornado over the last 10 years. All of these tornadoes started and stayed on land making a Sharknado impossible. Oklahoma has had plenty of tornadoes strong enough to lift and carry a shark but there are no sharks in Oklahoma besides in the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks, OK. California has not had a tornado above an EF2 over the last 10 years.


E.0.4 Conclusions
The probability of a Sharknado event is extremely low, if not a zero percent chance. There was one tornado in the three coastal states that might have had the ability to lift a shark. This South Carolina tornado happened to start and end on land making a Sharknado impossible. The Oklahoma Aquarium houses sharks in a state that is known for its amount and strengths of tornadoes. The Oklahoma Aquarium is in Tulsa County, OK where only EF2 or lower tornadoes have touched down in the last 10 years rendering this as very improbable.


E.0.5 Recommendations
From this study it is fairly certain that Sharknado’s are extremely unlikely if not a zero percent chance. Even though, strong storms and tornadoes without sharks are still a cause for concern. Property damage and their resulting insurance payouts will still be present with storms and tornadoes that have high wind speeds and with precipitaion events
